# Allergies and asthma

A reference for the family's allergy and asthma plans.

## Seasonal allergies

Pollen allergies respond to an oral antihistamine, a steroid nose spray used every day, and saline rinses. Keep windows closed on high-pollen days, shower before bed, and wash bedding weekly in hot water.

## Food allergy reactions

Hives, vomiting, a swollen lip or tingling in the mouth soon after eating a trigger food can be the start of a severe reaction. If breathing is affected or the person feels faint, use epinephrine immediately and call 911. Even if the person seems better afterward, they must go to the emergency department: a second wave of symptoms can follow hours later.

## Using an epinephrine auto-injector

Pull off the safety cap and press the tip firmly into the outer middle of the thigh, through clothing if needed, until it clicks. Hold it in place for 3 seconds. Rub the area for 10 seconds and call 911. If symptoms have not improved after 5 to 15 minutes, a second dose may be given.

## Asthma action plan

Green zone: no symptoms, take the daily controller. Yellow zone: cough, wheeze or tight chest; take 2 to 4 puffs of the quick-relief inhaler with a spacer and recheck in 20 minutes. Red zone: struggling to breathe, lips turning blue, or no relief after the inhaler. Call 911 and keep giving puffs every 20 minutes until help comes.

## Avoiding triggers

Dust mites, pet dander, mold, smoke and cold air all trigger asthma. Use allergen-proof pillow covers and keep pets out of the bedroom.
